In mentioning “questionable comments,” the FCC staffer quoted by-
Professor Weaver was presumably referring to “fake comments,” that is, 
“comments submitted by people or bots with either completely made up 
identifying information or real information belonging to a person who did 
not submit the comment.” Khtherine Krem, Crowdsourcing, Kind Of, 71 
Fe d . Co mmo n . L.J. 63, 66 (2018). Of the more than 22 million comments 
received in the 2017 net neutrality repeal proceeding:
“[A]t least 1.3 million comments were submitted using stolen 
or misused identities,” with more than 445,000 of these comments 
coming from Russian or German email accounts. Moreover, many 
comments were submitted by bots, which were detectable because 
they submitted duplicate comments differentiated only by the 
substitution of a synonym for a particular word.
Weaver, supra, at 561. With the revelation that so many comments in the 
rulemaking record were in some sense fraudulent, FCC Chairman Ajit Pai 
proposed in a July 6, 2018 letter to Senators Pat Toomey and Jeff Merkley, 
to “rebuild and reengineer” the FCC’s Electronic Comment Filing System, 
so long as Congress approved funding. He also sought to reassure the 
Senators that the FCC’s conclusions were not based on counting the 
number of comments for or against their proposal or on the identities of 
particular commenters.
Indeed, Chairman Pai’s Commission, in the preamble to its rule 
rescinding net neutrality, stated:
In reviewing the record in this rulemaking, the Commission 
complied with its obligations under the Administrative Procedure 
Act (APA), including the obligation to consider all “relevant 
matter” received, to adequately consider “important aspect[s] of 
the problem,” and to “reasonably respond to those comments that 
raise significant problems.” Consistent with these obligations, the 
Commission focused its review of the record on the submitted 
comments that bear substantively on the legal and public policy 
consequences of the actions we take today. Thus, our decision to 
restore internet freedom did not rely on comments devoid of 
substance, or the thousands of identical or nearly-identical non-
substantive comments that simply convey support or opposition to 
the proposals in the Internet Freedom NPRM.
Because we have complied with our obligations under the 
APA, we reject calls to delay adoption of this [rule] out of concerns 
that certain non-substantive comments (on which the Commission 
did not rely) may have been submitted under multiple different 
names or allegedly “fake” names.
83 Fed. Reg. 7913 (2018). Note how the familiar judicial demand that
